summary: This unit teaches you to shape (cut) hair safely and accurately: consult with the client, study the head, face and hair, choose a suitable shape, and cut it with scissors, clippers, trimmers and (on suitable hair) a razor. You will learn sectioning, elevation, guidelines and tension; the basic cuts (one-length, graduated, uniform layer and long layer); how to shape natural coily hair and give a clipper taper; and how to check the cut, keep your tools hygienic and keep records.

blocks.p: Hair shaping is the part of cosmetology that most clients notice first. A good cut suits the client's face, head and hair, holds its shape as it grows, and is easy for her to style at home. A bad cut cannot be put back: hair grows about 1 to 1.5 cm a month, so a mistake can take months to grow out. This unit is for COSMETOLOGY LEVEL 2 trainees, and it covers the whole job: consultation, tools, cutting method, natural hair, checking the cut, hygiene and records.

You will work with sharp blades close to a client's eyes, ears and neck, and with electric clippers. That is why the unit is about **safety and control** as much as about style: scissors closed when they are not cutting, clean and disinfected tools for every client, and a calm, planned way of working.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice, short answers and essays) and practical tasks in the Centre's salon. In the practicals you cut a one-length bob and a uniform layer cut on practice heads, and a tapered cut on short natural hair with clippers, scissor-over-comb and trimmers. The assessor watches your sectioning, elevation, guidelines, tool safety, cross-checking and clean-up, not only the finished shape.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: Photograph only the hair, your hands and the work area. Never photograph a client's or model's face unless she agrees and the Centre allows it.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Scissors and razors cut skin as easily as hair. Most accidents at the cutting station are nicks to the client's ear or neck, cuts to the stylist's own fingers, scissors dropped on feet, and trips and slips on cut hair. All of them are prevented by habits you learn now and keep for the rest of your career.

ul: Hold the scissors in your cutting hand: thumb in the thumb ring, ring finger in the finger ring, little finger on the tang (finger rest). Only the thumb moves to open and close the blades; the other blade stays still. This gives a clean, controlled cut.

**Palm the scissors** while you comb: close them, slip your thumb out of the ring and fold the closed scissors into your palm, held by the ring finger. The blades are then shut and away from the client while you comb and section.
Keep the blades **closed** whenever they are not cutting, especially near the ears, eyes and neck.
Pass scissors **closed, handles first**, into the other person's hand. Never throw or slide them, and never carry them in a pocket or hold them point-up when you walk.
Put them down closed, on the trolley, not on the chair or the floor. If scissors fall, **let them fall**: do not grab at them. Then clean and disinfect them before use.

Cut only hair with your cutting scissors. Paper, tape and neck strips blunt the blades. Blunt scissors chew and bend the hair instead of cutting it, and they push the hair, so the line comes out uneven. Report blunt or damaged scissors so they can be sharpened or replaced.

A salon razor (shaper) uses a replaceable blade and usually has a **guard**. Fit a new blade for each client; the used blade is single-use and goes straight into a **sharps box**, never into the ordinary bin.

Use a razor only on wet, straight or slightly wavy hair, with the blade stroked along the hair, never across it. On dry hair, or on curly and coily hair, a razor frays and roughens the ends and causes frizz.
Keep the guard on when the razor is not in your hand. Store it closed in its case.
Before use, check the **cord, plug and blades**: no frayed cord, cracked plug, loose or missing teeth. A damaged tool is not used; label it and report it.

Use electric tools with **dry hands**, away from basins and wet floors. Jamaica's supply is 110 V, 50 Hz; a tool bought abroad for 220 V or 60 Hz may run hot or badly, so use tools made for the Centre's sockets.
Switch off and unplug when you put the tool down, and never leave it switched on and hanging by the cord.
Keep the blades flat against the head and use the guard (attachment comb) for the length. Sharp corners of the blade cut the skin behind the ears and at the nape if you tilt them in.
Fold the ear forward and hold it with your free hand when you work round it.
A **neck strip** (paper or tissue) goes round the neck under the cape. It stops the cape, which is used for many clients, touching the skin, and it keeps cut hair out of the collar.
Fasten the cape so it is secure but not tight, with the client's collar tucked in.
Seat the client **upright**, feet flat on the footrest, legs uncrossed, head level. A tilted head or crossed legs tilt the shoulders and hips, and the cut comes out uneven.
Ask the client to take off earrings and glasses. Hold the ear and tell the client before you cut near it.
Brush cut hair off the face and neck with a clean neck brush, and keep hair out of the client's eyes.
Adjust the chair height so you work with a straight back and a clear view of the section: you should not stoop, twist or reach up.
Wear closed shoes: dropped scissors and clippers hurt.
Sweep up cut hair at once. Hair on a smooth floor is as slippery as water, it is unhygienic, and it gets into shoes and clothes. Wipe up water at once and put out a wet floor sign.
Short-cut hairs can pierce the skin between the fingers (a 'hair splinter'). Wash your hands and check them after every cut.

blocks.h: If you cut the client (or yourself)

flow: Stop cutting and stay calm; tell the client what happened
Put on gloves
Press a clean pad or tissue firmly on the cut until the bleeding stops
Cover it with a plaster if the client agrees
Tell the instructor or supervisor
Clean and disinfect any tool with blood on it before it is used again
Write it in the accident book

blocks.note: Blood can carry infections such as hepatitis B. Never touch another person's blood without gloves, never use a tool with blood on it on anyone else, and throw used pads and plasters into a bag that is tied and binned. A razor blade that has cut skin goes into the sharps box at once.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: Keep the first-aid kit, gloves and the accident book where every trainee can find them. In the Centre's salon, every cut is reported, however small: it is not a punishment, it is how the Centre keeps everyone safe.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Consultation: the head, the face and the hair

blocks.p: The consultation is where the cut is decided. Do it with the hair dry, in good light, at the styling chair, before you shampoo. Listen first, then look, then advise. Never start cutting until you and the client agree on the same picture.

flow: Greet the client and read her record card
Ask what she wants; use pictures to agree length and shape
Ask about her lifestyle, styling time and home care
Study the head form, face shape and growth patterns
Check texture, density, curl pattern and condition
Check the scalp for contra-indications
Advise, agree the plan, price and time
Record it

head: Ask about
Why it matters
rows: The length and shape she wants, with pictures
'A little off' means something different to every client. Agree a length in cm or by pointing to where it will sit (chin, shoulders, collar).
How much time she spends styling each day, and what tools she uses
A cut that needs a blow-dry every morning does not suit a client who wraps her hair and goes. The cut must suit the time she has to style it.
Her work, sport and hobbies
A nurse or chef may need hair that is off the face; a swimmer needs a cut that dries into shape.
Chemical services: relaxer, colour, texturiser, and when
Relaxed and lightened hair is weaker; a razor or heavy thinning can damage it. New growth changes how the hair falls.
How she will wear it: natural, pressed, blown out, in twists
Coily hair that will be worn stretched and hair that will be worn in its natural coil need different shapes.
Her last cut: what she liked and did not like
Tells you what to repeat and what to avoid.

blocks.h: The head form: landmarks you cut by

head: Landmark
Where it is
Why it matters in cutting
rows: Apex
The highest point on the top of the head.
The point from which hair is lifted straight up (180°) for long layers; the centre of a round shape.
Crown
The area behind the apex, where the hair often grows in a whorl.
Hair here changes direction; cut too short, it stands up.
Parietal ridge
The widest part of the head, around the top sides, where the head starts to curve in. Find it by laying a comb flat on the side of the head: where it leaves the head is the ridge.
Above the ridge the hair falls differently from below it. Many cuts change from graduation to layers here.
Occipital bone
The bone that sticks out at the back of the head, above the nape.
Hair above it falls over hair below it; a bob's weight line often sits at or just below it. Graduation is built up to it.
Nape
The back of the neck, at the lowest part of the hairline.
Where a one-length bob's guideline and a taper's shortest length start.
Hairline
The edge of the hair round the face, ears and nape.
The outline of the cut; where trimmers are used; where growth patterns show.
Temples
The sides of the forehead, above and in front of the ears.
Hair here is often finer and may recede; take care with short outlines.

blocks.p: The **oval** face is usually thought of as the balanced shape that suits most styles. For other shapes, the aim is to make the face look closer to an oval: add height or width where the face is short or narrow, and soften or cover where it is wide or long. Discuss it with the client; it is a guide, not a rule.

head: Face shape
What you see
Shapes that help
rows: Oval
Slightly longer than it is wide; balanced.
Most styles suit it.
Round
Full cheeks; width and length about equal.
Height on top, less width at the sides; length past the chin; a side part. Avoid width at the cheeks.
Square
Wide, straight jaw and forehead.
Soft layers round the face; height on top; avoid hard, straight lines at the jaw.
Oblong (long)
Longer than it is wide; narrow.
Width at the sides; a fringe (bangs) to shorten the face; avoid too much height on top.
Heart
Wide forehead, narrow chin.
Fullness at the jaw and chin; a side-swept fringe; avoid width at the temples.
Diamond
Narrow forehead and chin, wide cheekbones.
Fullness at the forehead and the jaw; a fringe; avoid width at the cheekbones.
Pear (triangle)
Narrow forehead, wide jaw.
Width and height on top; avoid width at the jaw.

blocks.p: Look at the whole head too: a flat back, a long neck, a high or low forehead, a prominent nose or ears. A cut can draw the eye towards or away from each of these. Hair that is cut short behind large ears shows them; hair left longer at the back fills out a flat back.

Hair does not grow straight out: it leans in a direction called its **natural fall**, and in some places it grows in strong patterns. Find them on dry hair before you cut, because they decide how short you can go.

head: Pattern
What it is
What to do
rows: Cowlick
A tuft of hair that grows in a different direction from the hair round it, often at the front hairline or the nape.
Do not cut it too short or against its direction: it will stick up. Leave a little extra length so its weight holds it down, or cut with the direction of growth.
Whorl
A circular, spiral growth pattern, usually at the crown.
Cut the crown with less tension and a little more length; short hair over a whorl stands up or parts on its own.
Double crown
Two whorls at the crown.
As for a whorl, with even more care about length.
Widow's peak
A front hairline that comes to a V-shaped point in the middle of the forehead.
A fringe cut straight across will split at the point; cut the fringe with the hair in its natural fall, or sweep it to one side.
Nape whorl or 'ducktail'
Hair at the nape that grows up, inwards or to one side.
Cut the nape in its natural direction; a tight outline here may not lie flat.
Receding hairline
The hairline moving back at the temples.
Keep the front soft; do not cut sharp lines that show the recession.

head: Check
What it means
Effect on the cut
rows: Texture
The thickness of one hair: fine, medium or coarse.
Fine hair shows every step and cannot take heavy thinning; coarse hair holds a line and may need weight removed.
Density
How many hairs grow on an area of scalp: low, medium or high.
High density needs thinner sections and more weight removal; low density needs blunt lines that keep weight.
Curl pattern
Straight, wavy, curly or coily.
Curly and coily hair shrinks as it dries; cut with little tension and often dry. Straight hair shows every unevenness, so lines must be clean.
Elasticity and condition
How well the hair stretches and returns; how damaged it is.
Weak, relaxed or lightened hair is cut with gentle tension and no razor.
Natural fall
The direction the hair lies when it is combed and left to settle.
For one-length cuts, comb into the natural fall and cut there; hair cut away from its fall springs back shorter than you planned.

blocks.h: Contra-indications: when you do not cut

head: Condition
What you see
What you do
rows: Head lice (pediculosis)
Small insects; oval eggs (nits) glued to the hairs near the scalp, at the nape and behind the ears.
Do not cut. Tell the client privately, suggest a pharmacist, and disinfect everything she touched.
Ringworm (tinea capitis)
Round, scaly patches; broken hairs or bald patches.
Do not cut. Refer her to a doctor.
Impetigo
Weeping sores with honey-coloured crusts.
Do not cut. Refer her to a doctor.
Open cuts, sores, boils or infected areas
Broken skin; red, painful lumps.
Do not cut over them; postpone or refer.
Severe psoriasis or eczema with broken skin
Thick scales or raw, weeping skin.
Postpone; refer. Mild, unbroken patches: cut gently.

blocks.note: Tell the client kindly and in private, without naming a disease; you are not a doctor. Advise her to see a doctor or pharmacist, book her back when it has cleared, and write it on the record card. Then clean and disinfect the chair, tools and the area, and bag the towels for a hot wash.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: Agree the length by showing it, not by saying it. Hold the dry hair where it will end and let the client see it in the mirror. Remember that wet hair looks longer, and curly hair looks longer wet than it will be dry.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Tool
What it is for
Notes
rows: Cutting scissors (shears)
The main cutting tool: blunt cutting, layering, point cutting, slide cutting, scissor-over-comb.
Usually 11.5 to 15 cm (4.5 to 6 inches). Longer blades for scissor-over-comb; shorter for detail. Keep them for hair only, dry them after disinfecting, and oil the pivot as the maker says.
Thinning (texturising) scissors
Remove bulk without changing the length much. One blade is toothed (fewer teeth remove more hair); some have teeth on both blades.
Use on the mid-lengths, never at the roots or on the hairline, and never on fine or thin hair. Work with the cut closed over the section once or twice, not again and again.
Razor (shaper)
Soft, tapered ends and thinned lengths on wet, straight hair.
Single-use blades into the sharps box. Not for dry, curly, coily, relaxed or damaged hair.
Clippers
Cut short hair fast and evenly; tapers and fades; shaping an afro outline.

Attachment combs (guards) leave the hair at a set, even length; numbers go up with length (a no. 1 is about 3 mm, a no. 4 about 13 mm, but check the maker's chart). The lever on many clippers opens or closes the blade a little for blending.
Trimmers (edgers, outliners)
Small clippers with a fine blade for sharp outlines round the hairline, ears and nape, and for detail.
Not for cutting bulk. Use them on dry hair with the skin held taut.
Cutting comb
Controls the section as you cut. Fine teeth for straight, smooth hair; wide teeth for curly and coily hair.
A long 'barber' comb is used for scissor-over-comb. The comb is held in the non-cutting hand while you cut; swap it to the cutting hand (with the scissors palmed) while you comb.
Afro comb (pick)
Lifts and separates coily hair without pulling it; used to pick an afro out evenly before and during shaping.
Metal or plastic; use with care near the scalp.
Wide-tooth comb
Detangling, especially coily and wet hair, from the ends up.
Combing from the roots drags small knots into big ones and breaks the hair.
Sectioning clips
Hold sections out of the way so you cut one section at a time.
Butterfly or duckbill clips; clean and disinfect them.
Water spray
Keeps the hair evenly damp during a wet cut.
Fresh water, clean bottle. Hair that dries while you cut shrinks and springs back, so the line comes out uneven.
Neck brush and neck strips
Brush cut hair off the skin; keep the cape off the neck.
Fresh neck strip for every client.
Cape (cutting gown), towels
Protect the client's clothes.
Fresh towel for every client; wipe or launder the cape.

ul: **Scissors:** after each client, wipe off the hair, wash or wipe clean, disinfect as the maker says (a spray or a short soak; many makers warn against long soaking, which corrodes the pivot), dry at once, and put a drop of oil on the pivot now and then. Store them closed in a case or a clean, covered drawer. Carry them in a case between the Centre and home.

**Clippers and trimmers:** brush the hair out of the blades with the small brush, spray the blades with a clipper disinfectant spray made for the purpose, wipe, then put a few drops of clipper oil on the blades and run the clipper for a few seconds so the oil spreads. Check the blades are aligned (the top blade level with and just behind the bottom blade) so they cannot cut the skin. Store with the cord loosely coiled, not wrapped tightly round the body.

**Combs and clips:** remove hair, wash in warm soapy water, soak in disinfectant for the contact time on the label, rinse if the label says, dry, and store covered. Throw away combs with broken teeth: they scratch the scalp.

blocks.note: Cleaning comes before disinfecting. Disinfectant cannot work through hair, grease and dirt, so a comb full of hair dropped into disinfectant comes out still full of germs. A UV cabinet only keeps clean, disinfected tools clean while they are stored.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: In Jamaica's humid climate, steel tools rust fast if they are put away wet. Dry scissors and clipper blades straight after disinfecting, and oil them.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Cutting principles: sections, elevation, guidelines and tension

blocks.p: Every cut, from a trim to a fade, is built from the same few ideas. Learn them well and you can understand any cut your instructor shows you.

ul: Sectioning divides the hair into clean, manageable parts so you can cut in a set order and see what you are doing. The common base is **four sections**: a centre parting from the front hairline to the nape, and a parting from ear to ear over the apex, giving two front and two back sections. Some cuts add a top (horseshoe) section around the parietal ridge.

Within a section you take **subsections**: thin slices of hair (about 0.5 to 1 cm, thinner for dense hair) that you can see through to the guide. A section you cannot see through is too thick, and the hair at the back of it will be cut longer than the hair at the front.

Partings are taken with the comb's tail or teeth: **horizontal** for one-length cuts and most graduation, **vertical** for layers, **diagonal** for soft, angled shapes. Keep the partings clean and the clipped sections out of the way.

blocks.p: **Elevation** is the angle at which you lift the hair away from the head before you cut it. It is measured from the head, so 0° is hair lying flat and 90° is hair held straight out. The more you lift, the more layered the shape and the less weight is left at the bottom.

head: Elevation
How the hair is held
What it gives
Typical cut
rows: 0° (no elevation)
Combed down flat in its natural fall and cut at the bottom.
All hair ends on one line: full weight at the bottom, a strong **weight line**.
One-length (blunt, club) cut, bob, blunt fringe.
Low to medium (about 30° to 60°, often called 45°)
Lifted a little away from the head.
**Graduation**: hair at the nape is shortest and each section above is a little longer, so the ends stack up and build weight in a rounded shape.
Graduated bob; the back of many short cuts.
90° (from the curve of the head)
Held straight out from the head where the section grows, following the curve.
**Uniform layers**: every hair about the same length; no weight build-up; a round shape that follows the head.
Uniform layer cut; a rounded afro shape.
180° (straight up from the apex)
All hair combed straight up to the top of the head and cut there.
**Long layers**: shortest on top and longer underneath; movement with length kept.
Long layered cut.

blocks.note: The guide you hold matters as much as the angle. At 90° from the curve of the head, hair at the nape is held out sideways, hair at the crown is held up. If you hold every section straight up instead, the nape hair is over-directed and ends up longer: that is 180° long layering, not uniform layers.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: A **guideline** (guide) is the first section you cut to the agreed length. Every section after it is cut to match the guide, so the guide sets the length for the rest of the cut. Cut it slowly and check it before you go on.

A **stationary guide** stays in one place and every section is brought to it. It is used for one-length cuts (the nape guide), for most graduation, and for long layers (hair brought up to a guide at the apex). The further a section is from the guide, the longer it ends up, which is how weight builds.

A **travelling (moving) guide** moves with you: after you cut one section, a thin slice of it becomes the guide for the next. It is used for uniform layers and anywhere the length should be the same all over.
Always see the guide through the section. If you cannot see it, your section is too thick: take less hair.

**Tension** is how tightly you hold the hair between your fingers as you cut. **Even tension** on every section gives an even line. Too much tension stretches the hair, which springs back shorter when you let go; this is worst on curly and coily hair, around the ears, and at the hairline. For a blunt bob, use the comb to hold the hair and cut below it with very little tension.

**Over-direction** is combing the hair away from its natural fall, towards a guide, before you cut. Hair over-directed to a guide behind it comes out longer at the front; over-directed forward, it comes out longer at the back. It is used on purpose to build length or weight, and by accident when you comb carelessly, so comb every section the same way.

The **cutting line** (finger angle) is the angle of your fingers, and so of the cut, across the section: horizontal gives a straight line, diagonal forward gives a shape longer at the front, diagonal back gives a shape longer at the back.

head: Cutting on
Good for
Take care
rows: Wet (evenly damp) hair
Straight, wavy and relaxed hair; precise lines; one-length and layered cuts.
Keep it evenly damp with the spray: hair that dries as you cut shrinks and the line comes out uneven. Wet hair stretches, so leave a little extra length.
Dry hair
Curly and coily hair in its natural state; afro shaping; clipper work; final refining of any cut.
You see the true shape and length after shrinkage. Clean, detangled hair only; no heavy product.

ul: The **weight line** is the line in a cut where its weight sits: the bottom edge of a bob, or the point where graduation stops building. A clean weight line makes a cut look finished and 'expensive'; steps or holes in it look like a mistake.

**Balance** means both sides match: the same length at the ears, the cheekbones and the jaw, and the same shape when you look at the head from the front and the back. Check it often from a step back, and in the mirror.

blocks.note: Keep the client's head level. Every time she looks down at her phone, or tilts to talk, the line you are cutting tilts with her. Ask her kindly to look straight ahead, and check her head position before every section at the back and the sides.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Cutting techniques and the basic cuts

head: Technique
How it is done
Result and use
rows: Blunt (club) cutting
The section is combed smooth and cut straight across with the scissors closing fully.
Clean, solid ends and a strong line; keeps weight. The base of most cuts; bobs and fringes.
Point cutting
The tips of the scissors cut into the ends of the section at an angle.
Softens a line, takes out hard edges, blends and adds texture. Used on dry or damp hair at the end of a cut.
Slide (slice) cutting
Partly open scissors slide along the hair from the mid-lengths towards the ends.
Removes length and bulk with a soft, tapered effect; blends long layers. Sharp scissors only, and never on damaged hair.
Scissor-over-comb
The comb lifts the hair away from the head at the angle wanted, and the scissors cut the hair that sticks out above the comb, moving up the head with the comb.
Short, blended shapes on short hair: napes, sides, blending a clipper taper into longer hair above.
Clipper cutting
The clipper with a guard (or an open blade) is moved against the growth, flat to the head.
Fast, even short lengths; tapers and fades. Clipper-over-comb works like scissor-over-comb for blending.
Thinning
Thinning scissors close once or twice over the mid-lengths of a section.
Removes bulk, not length; lets thick hair lie flatter. Keep away from the roots, the hairline and fine hair.
Razor cutting
The razor is stroked down the hair at a shallow angle, on wet straight hair.
Soft, wispy, tapered ends; thins as it cuts. Not for curly, coily, relaxed or dry hair.
Freehand
Cutting without holding the hair between the fingers, for example trimming an afro's outline with scissors or clippers.
Shaping natural hair and finishing outlines.

flow: Consult, shampoo, comb the damp hair smooth and seat the client upright with her head level
Section into four; clip the top sections away
At the nape, take a thin horizontal section and comb it down into its natural fall
Hold it against the skin with the comb (or lightly between your fingers at 0°) and cut the guideline straight across at the agreed length
Check the guide is level from both sides before you go on
Bring down the next thin horizontal section, comb it over the guide and cut it to the same line
Work up the back to the occipital bone, keeping the head level and the hair evenly damp
Release the sides; take horizontal sections from the back guide forward and cut them to join the back line
Keep the tension light round the ears, where the hair sits over the ear and springs up when it is released
Cross-check with vertical sections, dry the hair, check the line in the mirror on both sides and refine

blocks.p: A one-length cut has a **stationary guide** at the nape; every section is combed down to it. Because the hair falls in a curve over the head, a bob cut this way looks slightly longer at the front than at the back, which is the classic bob shape. For a straight-across look, or a longer front (an 'A-line'), change the cutting line at the sides.

ul: Start at the nape with a narrow guide cut short. Take thin horizontal or diagonal sections, lift each one to the same low angle (about 45°), and cut parallel to the head shape, with the previous section as your guide.
Because each section is lifted, the hair above ends a little longer than the hair below: the ends **stack**, building a curved **weight line** up to the occipital bone.
Stop building weight where the shape needs its fullest point (often around the occipital bone), then layer or leave the hair above it to fall over the graduation.
Graduation suits clients who want shape and fullness at the back, for example a graduated bob that is short at the nape and longer to the front.

Cut a guide on the top (apex) at the length wanted, then take **vertical sections** from the crown to the nape and round the head. Hold each section straight out from the curve of the head (90°) and cut it to the **travelling guide** from the section before.

Every hair ends up about the same length, so there is no weight line and the shape follows the round of the head. It gives even movement all over and suits short to medium cuts on straight, wavy and (worn stretched) relaxed hair.
Work in an even order, for example from the front to the back on one side, then the other, and cross-check with horizontal sections.
Cut a guide on the top, then bring sections from the sides and back **straight up to the apex** (180°) and cut them to that stationary guide.

Hair that grows further from the apex (at the nape and the ends at the sides) has further to travel, so it ends longer. The result is shorter on top and longer underneath: movement and softness without losing the length.
Blend the layers into the length with point cutting or slide cutting on dry hair.
Take a triangle section from the front hairline back towards the apex; the deeper the section, the fuller the fringe.

Comb the hair into its natural fall. Cut a blunt fringe at 0° with **no tension**, a little longer than you think: wet hair, a cowlick and a widow's peak all make a fringe spring up shorter when it dries.
Point-cut the ends on dry hair to soften.

blocks.note: Cut a little less than the agreed length first. You can always take more off; you can never put it back. Show the client the length in the mirror before the final line, especially on the fringe and round the face.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Fault
Likely cause
Cure or prevention
rows: One side of a bob longer than the other
The client's head was tilted; uneven tension; the sides were not brought to the same guide.
Level the head; comb and hold both sides the same way; compare the same points in the mirror; cut the longer side to match, never 'chase' both sides down.
Steps or holes in a one-length line
Sections too thick; hair dried while cutting; hair over-directed.
Thin sections, even dampness, comb into natural fall; refine on dry hair.
Hair springs up shorter at the ears or fringe
Too much tension over the ear or on a cowlick.
Little or no tension there; leave extra length.
Corners (a 'shelf') in layers
Elevation changed between sections; guide not seen.
Keep the same angle; take thinner sections; cross-check.
Frizzy, frayed ends
Blunt scissors; razor or thinning scissors on curly, coily or damaged hair.
Sharp scissors; blunt or point cutting only on textured hair.
Lines in a clipper taper
Guard changed without blending; clipper tilted into the head.
Blend with the lever, clipper-over-comb or scissor-over-comb; keep the blade flat.
Hair sticks up at the crown or front
Cut too short over a whorl or cowlick.
Leave more length and cut with the direction of growth; next time, check growth patterns first.

blocks.p: Most clients in a Jamaican salon have curly or coily hair, worn natural, stretched, relaxed, in locs or under a protective style. Shaping it well is a skill that clients come back for. Two things make it different from cutting straight hair: **shrinkage** and **fragility**.

ul: Coily hair can look half its true length, or less, when it dries and springs up. Wet hair that is stretched out and cut to 'shoulder length' can sit at the ears when it dries.
So: cut with **very little tension**, and whenever the client wears her hair in its natural state, shape it **dry**, in the way she wears it, so you see the real shape and length.
If she wears it stretched or blown out, you can cut it stretched (blown out or on a low-heat blow-dry), but agree with her first how she will wear it most of the time.
Explain shrinkage to the client during the consultation, so she is not surprised when the dry length is shorter than the wet length.

Every bend in a coil is a weak point. Detangle **from the ends up**, with conditioner or a leave-in for slip, using your fingers first and then a wide-tooth comb or pick. Never drag a fine comb from the roots.
Work in small sections and keep the clipped sections twisted so they do not re-tangle.
Use sharp scissors and blunt or point cutting. Razors and thinning scissors fray the coil and cause frizz and split ends.
Trim only what is needed: split, thin, see-through ends and single-strand knots. Clients who are growing their hair want the shape kept with the least length taken.

flow: Consult; check the scalp and growth patterns; agree the size and shape
Detangle gently from the ends with a wide-tooth comb, then pick the dry hair out evenly all over with an afro comb
Stand back and look at the outline from the front, the sides and the back
Trim the outline freehand with scissors (or clippers, carefully) in small amounts, working round the head and keeping the shape rounded and even
Pick the hair out again and step back often: picking shows the hairs that are still too long
Keep the perimeter in balance with the face: fuller on top for a round face, fuller at the sides for a long face
Outline the hairline, nape and sideburns with trimmers if the client wants a clean edge
Brush off the cut hair, show the client the shape with a hand mirror, and refine

blocks.h: A tapered cut on short natural hair

blocks.p: A **taper** is shortest at the nape and the hairline and gets gradually longer going up the head, blending into the length on top. A **fade** is a taper taken down to the skin at the bottom. Both are cut with clippers and guards, blended with the clipper lever, clipper-over-comb or scissor-over-comb, and finished with trimmers.

flow: Consult; check the scalp; agree the lengths on top, at the sides and at the nape
Check the clipper cord, plug and blades; dry hands; dry, detangled, picked-out hair
Set the length on top first with scissors or the largest guard, so you know what you are blending into
Start at the nape and sides with a short guard (for example a no. 1 or 2), working up against the growth, flat to the head, and stop at the line where the next length begins
Change to the next larger guard and work up a little higher, blending the line between the two lengths; repeat up to the top length
Use the lever, clipper-over-comb or scissor-over-comb to smooth any lines, flicking the clipper away from the head as you reach the top of each stroke
Outline the hairline, round the ears and the nape with trimmers, with the skin held taut
Cross-check the balance of both sides and the back; show the client with a hand mirror

ul: **Guard numbers:** the smaller the number, the shorter the hair. Always check the chart for the clippers you are using, because numbers and lengths differ between makers.
**Work against the growth** to lift the hair into the blade; a pass with the growth leaves hair behind.
**Blend a little at a time.** It is much easier to take the taper higher than to grow it back.
**Growth patterns:** a nape whorl or a cowlick at the front can leave a bald-looking patch if the taper is cut too close over it. Keep a little length there.

head: Service
How it is shaped
Notes
rows: Trim on stretched natural hair
Blow out on low heat, then cut in sections with light tension, often at 90° or 180° for shape.
Protect the hair with a heat protectant; agree that the cut will look different in its natural state.
Trim on relaxed hair
Cut damp like straight hair: one-length, graduation or layers.
Relaxed hair is weaker, especially at the line of demarcation; no razor, light tension, sharp scissors.
Trimming locs
Trim the ends to even the length, one loc at a time, with sharp scissors, usually on dry locs.
Never cut into the body of a loc. Ask before trimming: many clients keep their locs for religious or cultural reasons.
Shaping a twist-out or curly cut
Cut dry, curl by curl, in the pattern the hair is worn, removing length where the curls sit too long.
Takes time; small amounts at a time.
Children's cuts
Short, quick sections; keep scissors closed near the face; a parent beside the chair.
Children move: cut with the blades pointing away from the face and ears.

blocks.note: Ask how the client wants her hair handled, and respect it. A client with locs, a client who covers her hair, and a client growing out a relaxer each have reasons for what they want. Advise honestly, then do what she agrees to.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.note: Ask the client to take off earrings before a clipper taper or a trimmer outline: hoops catch in combs and trimmers and can tear the ear.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: **Cross-check** by taking sections in the opposite direction to the ones you cut with: vertical sections to check a cut made with horizontal sections, and horizontal to check vertical ones. Hold each section at the same elevation you cut at. An even line through the cross-check means the cut is even; long hairs show as 'spikes' sticking past the line.
**Compare both sides** in the mirror, at the same points: the length at the ears, the cheekbones, the jaw, and the nape corners. Check with the client's head level and from a step back.
**Check the weight line** or the graduation for steps and holes, and run your comb through to feel for long hairs.
**Check the outline:** the nape, round the ears and the fringe should be clean, even and in balance.

**Dry and check again.** Hair looks different dry: a straight bob shows every unevenness, and curly hair shrinks into its real shape. Make small corrections on dry hair with point cutting or scissor-over-comb.
**Show the client the back** with a hand mirror, and ask if she is happy before she leaves the chair.

blocks.note: Correct an uneven cut by bringing the longer side to the shorter side, once. Cutting a little off each side in turn ('chasing') makes the cut shorter and shorter without ever matching.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Brush all the cut hair off the face, neck and cape with the neck brush; remove the neck strip and shake out the cape away from the client.
Style the hair as agreed: blow-dry, set, wrap, twist or pick out. Use a heat protectant on heat styling.

Give **home-care advice**: how to style the shape, which products suit it, and when to come back. Most cuts keep their shape for about 4 to 8 weeks; short cuts and tapers need trimming more often (often every 2 to 4 weeks), long hair can go 8 to 12 weeks. Say when and book it.
Tell the client the price, and note any products she buys.

flow: Sweep up all the cut hair and bin it
Clean and disinfect the scissors, combs and clips; brush, disinfect and oil the clippers and trimmers
Fit a new razor blade; put the used one in the sharps box
Wipe the chair, trolley and mirror with disinfectant
Put the towel in the closed laundry bin; wipe or launder the cape
Wipe up any water; check the floor is dry
Wash your hands and check them for hair splinters
Lay out clean tools for the next client

head: Word
Meaning
rows: Cleaning
Removing hair, dirt, grease and product with detergent and water. Always first.
Disinfecting
Using a chemical, made up and timed as the label says, to kill most harmful germs on clean tools and surfaces.
Contact time
How long the tool or surface must stay wet with the disinfectant for it to work: the time on the label, often several minutes.
Sterilising
Killing all germs and their spores (for example in an autoclave). Used for tools that break the skin; not usual for scissors and combs.
Single-use
Used once and thrown away: razor blades, neck strips, some gloves and pads.

head: What to record
Example
rows: Date, client's name and contact details
07/11/2026, Kerry-Ann Thompson, May Pen
Consultation findings
Round face; cowlick at front hairline; medium texture, high density, coily; worn stretched
Scalp
Clear; no contra-indications
The cut
Blow-out trim, uniform layers at 90°, about 2 cm removed; fringe left longer over cowlick
Tools and techniques
Scissors, blunt and point cutting; trimmers on nape
Problems or accidents
None
Advice and next visit
Trim in 8 weeks; leave-in and heat protectant for blow-outs
Stylist
J. Brown (trainee), checked by the instructor

blocks.note: Client records are personal information and are kept private and secure under Jamaica's Data Protection Act. Do not share a client's details, or photographs of her, without her permission.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: I can hold, palm, pass and store scissors safely, and say why blades stay closed when they are not cutting.
I can fit and dispose of a razor blade safely, and say which hair a razor must not be used on.
I can check clippers before use, and use them with dry hands away from water.
I can protect the client with a neck strip and cape and seat her upright with her head level.
I can deal with a cut to a client: gloves, pressure, plaster, report, accident book, and disinfecting the tool.
I can carry out a consultation and agree the length and shape with pictures.
I can name the apex, crown, parietal ridge, occipital bone, nape and hairline and say why each matters.
I can describe the main face shapes and suggest shapes that suit them.
I can recognise a cowlick, a whorl, a double crown and a widow's peak and allow for them.
I can check texture, density, curl pattern and natural fall and say how each affects the cut.
I can recognise lice, ringworm, impetigo and open wounds, and refer the client tactfully.
I can name the main tools and say what each is for and how to clean, disinfect and oil it.
I can section hair cleanly and take sections I can see through.
I can explain elevation at 0°, 45°, 90° and 180° and the shape each gives.
I can explain stationary and travelling guides, tension, over-direction and the cutting line.
I can describe blunt, point, slide, scissor-over-comb, clipper, thinning and razor cutting.
I can cut a one-length bob, a graduated shape, uniform layers and long layers.
I can explain shrinkage and cut coily hair with little tension, often dry.
I can pick out and shape an afro, and give a clipper taper blended with scissor-over-comb and outlined with trimmers.
I can cross-check a cut, compare both sides, refine on dry hair and show the client the back.
I can clean up, keep tools hygienic, give aftercare advice and fill in the record card.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give the reason for each step. For example: 'I take thin sections I can see through, so that every hair reaches the guide and the line is even.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: Hair shaping
Cutting hair to a planned shape that suits the client's head, face and hair.
Apex
The highest point on the top of the head.
Crown
The area behind the apex, where a whorl is often found.
Parietal ridge
The widest part of the head, around the top sides, where the head begins to curve in.
Occipital bone
The bone that sticks out at the back of the head, above the nape.
Nape
The back of the neck, at the lowest part of the hairline.
Hairline
The edge of the hair round the face, ears and neck; the outline of a cut.
Natural fall
The direction the hair lies when it is combed and left to settle.
Growth pattern
A direction in which hair grows strongly in one place: cowlick, whorl, double crown, widow's peak.
Cowlick
A tuft of hair growing in a different direction from the hair round it.
Whorl
A circular, spiral growth pattern, usually at the crown.
Widow's peak
A front hairline that comes to a V-shaped point in the middle of the forehead.
Texture
The thickness of one hair: fine, medium or coarse.
Density
How many hairs grow on an area of scalp.
Shrinkage
The way curly and coily hair springs up and looks shorter as it dries.
Sectioning
Dividing the hair into clean parts so it is cut in a set order.
Subsection
A thin slice of a section, thin enough to see the guide through.
Elevation
The angle the hair is lifted from the head before it is cut.
One-length (blunt) cut
A cut at 0° where all the hair ends on one line, with a strong weight line.
Graduation
A cut at low to medium elevation where the hair gets longer going up and the ends stack to build weight.
Uniform layers
A cut at 90° from the curve of the head, with all the hair about the same length.
Long layers
A cut at 180°, held up to the apex, shorter on top and longer underneath.
Guideline (guide)
The first section cut to the agreed length, which the other sections are cut to match.
Stationary guide
A guide that stays in one place; every section is brought to it.
Travelling guide
A guide that moves with you: part of each cut section guides the next.
Tension
How tightly the hair is held as it is cut; it must be even and, on curly hair, light.
Over-direction
Combing the hair away from its natural fall towards a guide before cutting.
Cutting line
The angle of the fingers (and so of the cut) across a section.
Weight line
The line in a cut where its weight sits, such as the bottom edge of a bob.
Cross-checking
Checking a cut by taking sections in the opposite direction to the ones it was cut with.
Blunt (club) cutting
Cutting straight across a section so the ends are solid.
Point cutting
Cutting into the ends with the tips of the scissors to soften a line.
Slide cutting
Sliding partly open scissors along the hair to remove length and bulk softly.
Scissor-over-comb
Lifting hair with a comb and cutting what sticks out above it, moving up the head.
Clipper guard (attachment comb)
A comb that clips onto the clipper to leave the hair at a set length.
Taper
A cut that is shortest at the nape and hairline and gets longer going up.
Fade
A taper that goes down to the skin at the bottom.
Trimmers (edgers)
Small clippers with a fine blade for sharp outlines.
Thinning scissors
Scissors with a toothed blade that remove bulk without changing the length much.
Razor (shaper)
A guarded razor with a single-use blade for soft, tapered ends on wet straight hair.
Sharps box
A sealed container for used blades.
Neck strip
A paper or tissue strip round the neck that keeps the cape off the skin.
Contra-indication
Anything that means the service should not go ahead or must be changed.
Disinfecting
Killing most harmful germs on clean tools with a chemical, for the contact time on the label.
Accident book
The record in which every accident, including a cut, is written down.

c1.title: A nurse's bob in Portmore
c1.text: Nurse Kadian Lewis, 31, comes to a salon in Portmore. Her relaxed hair is just past her shoulders and she wants it cut to chin length, blunt, so it dries quickly and stays off her collar on the ward. She has a round face and a strong cowlick at the front hairline on the left. Trainee Shereen shampoos her, seats her, and starts to section. Halfway up the back, Kadian takes out her phone and tilts her head down to read a message while Shereen keeps cutting.

c2.title: An afro shape in Half Way Tree
c2.text: Monique Gayle, 24, wears her natural coily hair in a rounded afro. At a salon in Half Way Tree she asks for the shape to be evened up but 'not much shorter'. Trainee Andre shampoos her, combs the wet hair out straight, pulls each section taut and cuts it to the length they agreed in the mirror while it was wet. When the hair dries and springs up, it sits well above her ears and Monique is upset.

c3.title: A taper for a schoolboy in Linstead
c3.text: Mrs Grant brings her son Jaden, 12, to a salon in Linstead for a tapered cut before the new term. Trainee Ricardo picks up the clippers and notices the cord is frayed near the plug, with a little copper wire showing. The only other clippers are being used. While Ricardo is outlining behind Jaden's ear with the trimmers, Jaden jerks his head and the blade nicks the skin behind his ear; a small drop of blood appears.

c4.title: Long layers for a visitor in Negril
c4.text: Emma, a visitor from Canada staying at a hotel in Negril, has fine, straight, shoulder-length hair with low density. She asks for long layers 'for movement' and mentions that a stylist at home once used thinning scissors and 'took out half my hair'. Trainee Tanisha wets the hair, but by the time she reaches the second side it is almost dry and the first layers she cut look longer than the ones she is cutting now.

c5.title: Practice heads in the Savanna-la-Mar training salon
c5.text: In the Centre's training salon in Savanna-la-Mar, two trainees share a cutting station. Devon cuts a uniform layer cut on a practice head, holding every section straight up towards the ceiling. He finishes and asks Alicia to pass her scissors so he can refine the nape; she tosses them across the trolley. Later, the instructor checks Devon's cut and finds the nape hair longer than the top.

questions.q: Which elevation and guide should Shereen use to cut Kadian's blunt, chin-length bob?
o: 0°, with a stationary guide cut at the nape
45°, with a stationary guide cut at the nape
90°, with a travelling guide cut at the apex
180°, with a stationary guide cut at the apex
questions.why: A one-length (blunt) cut is made at 0°: each section is combed down into its natural fall and cut to the stationary guideline at the nape, so all the hair ends on one line with a strong weight line.

questions.q: What should Shereen do about the cowlick at Kadian's front hairline?
o: Cut it to the same chin length as the rest, with firm tension
Thin it out with thinning scissors so it lies flat
Leave it a little longer and cut with its direction of growth
Cut it shorter than the rest so it blends into the line
questions.why: A cowlick grows in its own direction and springs up when it is cut short or against its growth. Extra length gives it weight to hold it down; cutting with the growth direction keeps the line even.

questions.q: What is likely to happen if Shereen keeps cutting while Kadian reads her phone with her head tilted down?
o: The line at the back will come out uneven once her head is level again
The hair will dry faster, so the sections will shrink and spring up
The sections will be over-directed forward and end longer at the front
The guideline will stretch under the extra tension and be cut too short
questions.why: The cut follows the position of the head. Sections cut while the head is tilted sit at a different angle when the head is level, so the line comes out crooked. Ask the client to look straight ahead and check her head before every section.

questions.q: Kadian's round face is best balanced by which kind of shape?
o: Width at the cheeks and a straight, full fringe
Height on top, less width at the sides, length past the chin
Fullness at the jaw and a short, rounded outline at the ears
An even, rounded shape with equal width and height
questions.why: A round face is about as wide as it is long, so the aim is to make it look longer and slimmer: height on top, length below the chin and less width at the cheeks. Width at the cheeks or a rounded shape makes it look rounder.

questions.q: Why did Monique's afro end up so much shorter than she expected?
o: Coily hair stretched wet and cut taut shrinks a great deal as it dries
Shampooing coily hair before a cut makes the coils tighten for good
Cutting wet hair always takes off twice the length that was agreed
The scissors were blunt, so they pushed the hair and cut it too short
questions.why: Coily hair can shrink to half its stretched length or less as it dries. Hair that was pulled straight and cut while wet springs up far above the agreed length. Cut coily hair with little tension, and shape it dry when it is worn natural.

questions.q: How should Andre have shaped Monique's afro?
o: Blow-dried it straight, then cut it all with firm tension at 90°
Picked the dry hair out evenly and trimmed the outline freehand, checking often
Combed it wet in four sections and cut each to a nape guide at 0° with light tension
Thinned the whole head with thinning scissors to even up the shape and the length
questions.why: An afro worn natural is shaped dry, in its natural state: pick it out evenly, trim the outline in small amounts, pick again and step back often. That way you see the real shape and length. Thinning scissors fray coily hair.

questions.q: Before combing Monique's coily hair, what is the safest way to detangle it?
o: With a fine-tooth cutting comb from the roots down, in a few large sections
With a razor comb from the mid-lengths, to cut out the knots as it goes along
With a wide-tooth comb or fingers from the ends up, with slip from conditioner
With a dry afro pick pulled firmly from the scalp outwards through the hair
questions.why: Every bend in a coil is a weak point. Detangling from the ends up, in small sections and with slip from conditioner, undoes small knots before they become big ones; combing from the roots drags knots together and breaks the hair.

questions.q: What should Ricardo do about the clippers with the frayed cord?
o: Wrap tape round the frayed part and use them until the other pair is free
Not use them, label them faulty and report them, then wait for safe clippers
Use them, but keep the plug end well away from the client's head
Use them unplugged for the outline only, then charge them up later
questions.why: A cord with bare wire showing can give a shock or start a fire. A damaged electric tool is taken out of use, labelled and reported; it is never patched with tape. Wait for, or borrow, a tool that passes the check.

questions.q: What should Ricardo do first after the trimmer nicks the skin behind Jaden's ear?
o: Finish the outline quickly so the cut does not look uneven, then look at the nick
Wipe the blood with the neck brush and carry on, as it is only a small drop
Stop, put on gloves and press a clean pad on the nick until it stops bleeding
Spray the nick with clipper disinfectant to kill any germs on the skin
questions.why: Stop at once and deal with the injury: gloves first, then firm pressure with a clean pad, then a plaster if the parent agrees. Clipper disinfectant is for blades, not skin. Then report it and write it in the accident book.

questions.q: What must happen to the trimmer that nicked Jaden before it is used on anyone else?
o: Its blade must be brushed free of hair and oiled as usual
It must be put in the UV cabinet for the rest of the day
It must be cleaned and then disinfected, because it has blood on it
It must be sent for sharpening, because a sharp blade does not nick
questions.why: Blood can carry infections such as hepatitis B. Any tool that has touched blood is cleaned and then disinfected as the maker says before it is used again. A UV cabinet does not disinfect, and oiling alone does nothing to germs.

questions.q: Ricardo starts Jaden's taper at the nape with a no. 1 guard and wants the hair longer going up the head. What should he do next?
o: Keep the no. 1 guard and tilt the clipper into the head as he goes higher
Switch to a smaller guard higher up and blend with trimmers
Change to the next larger guard, work a little higher and blend the line
Take the guard off and use the open blade above the nape line
questions.why: A taper gets longer going up, so each step up the head uses a larger guard, and the line between two lengths is blended with the lever, clipper-over-comb or scissor-over-comb. A smaller guard or an open blade makes it shorter, and tilting the blade cuts the skin.

questions.q: Which elevation gives Emma the long layers she wants while keeping her length?
o: Hair combed down flat and cut at 0° to a nape guide
Hair lifted to 45° and cut parallel to the head from the nape
Hair held out at 90° from the curve of the head with a travelling guide
Hair brought straight up to the apex at 180° and cut to a stationary guide
questions.why: Long layers are cut at 180°: every section is combed up to a guide at the apex, so hair that grows further from the apex ends longer. The result is shorter on top and longer underneath, with the length kept.

questions.q: Why is Tanisha's second side coming out shorter than the first, and what should she do?
o: The hair dried and shrank, so she should spray it evenly damp again
The hair stretched when wet, so she should use more tension on side two
The guide moved, so she should cut a new, shorter guide on side one
The sections were too thin, so she should take thicker ones on side two
questions.why: Hair that dries while you cut springs back shorter, so sections cut dry do not match sections cut wet. Keep the whole head evenly damp with the water spray. Re-cutting the first side shorter would 'chase' the cut shorter and shorter.

questions.q: Emma's hair is fine with low density. Which is the best way to blend her layers softly?
o: Thinning scissors closed several times through each section at the roots
Point cutting on the ends of the dry hair with sharp scissors
A razor stroked across the dry sections to taper them
Blunt cutting each layer at 90° to keep all the weight
questions.why: Fine, low-density hair cannot spare bulk: thinning scissors and a razor would leave it thinner and wispy, and a razor is used along wet hair, never across dry hair. Point cutting softens the layer lines while keeping the weight she has.

questions.q: Why is the nape hair on Devon's practice head longer than the top?
o: He used a stationary guide at the nape instead of at the apex
He held every section straight up, which over-directed the lower hair to 180°
He took sections that were too thin, so the guide was always visible
He cut the top first, so the travelling guide got longer as he worked down
questions.why: Uniform layers are cut at 90° from the curve of the head: nape hair is held out sideways, crown hair up. Holding every section straight up to the ceiling is 180°: the nape hair travels further to reach the guide and ends longer, which is long layering, not uniform layers.

questions.q: How should Alicia have handed her scissors to Devon?
o: Open, blades towards him, so he can slip his fingers straight into the rings
Closed, handles first, placed into his hand
Slid along the trolley, closed, so neither of them touches the blades
Closed, points first, held by the handles so she keeps control of the rings
questions.why: Scissors are passed closed, with the handles towards the other person, placed into the hand. Tossing or sliding them can cut someone or damage the blades, and open or point-first passing puts the blades at the receiver's fingers.

questions.q: Devon cut his layers with vertical sections. How should he cross-check the cut?
o: Take vertical sections again and hold them at a lower elevation
Take horizontal sections and hold them at the same elevation he cut at
Comb all the hair down to 0° and check that the ends make one line
Pick the hair out with an afro comb and look at the outline from the front
questions.why: Cross-checking means taking sections in the opposite direction to the cutting sections, held at the elevation the cut was made at. Long hairs then stick out past the line and can be corrected. Combing to 0° only checks a one-length cut.

questions.q: A stylist finds the widest part of a client's head by laying a comb flat against the side of the head and noting where it leaves the skull. What has she found?
o: The occipital bone
The apex
The parietal ridge
The crown
questions.why: The parietal ridge is the widest part of the head, around the top sides, where the head begins to curve in. A comb laid flat on the side leaves the head there. The occipital bone is at the back, and the apex and crown are on top.

questions.q: A stylist has a thin sliver of hair from each section she has just cut guiding the next section, all the way round the head. What kind of guide is she using, and for what cut does it suit best?
o: A stationary guide, for a one-length bob
A stationary guide, for long layers
A travelling guide, for graduation at the nape
A travelling guide, for uniform layers
questions.why: A guide that moves with you, where part of each cut section guides the next, is a travelling guide. It gives the same length everywhere, which is exactly what uniform layers at 90° need. One-length cuts and long layers use a stationary guide.

questions.q: A client with dry, coily natural hair asks for soft, wispy ends like a picture of a razor cut she has seen. What should the stylist advise?
o: A razor on wet hair gives the same soft result on every hair type
A razor would fray her coils; point cutting with sharp scissors is gentler
Thinning scissors at the roots will give the wispy look without a razor
The hair must be relaxed first, because coily hair cannot be shaped at all
questions.why: A razor suits wet, straight hair only. On dry, curly or coily hair it frays and roughens the ends, causing frizz and split ends. Sharp scissors with blunt or point cutting keep coily ends smooth; thinning at the roots damages any hair.
